title: King Lear
author: William Shakespeare
openingChapterLabel: Act 1, Scene 1 — A Room of State in King Lear's Palace
about:
Lear, the old king of Britain, decides to retire and divide his kingdom among his three daughters according to how well each one says she loves him. His two older daughters, Goneril and Regan, deliver elaborate flattering speeches. His youngest, Cordelia, refuses to play and is disinherited. The Earl of Kent objects and is banished. Cordelia leaves with the King of France, who marries her without a dowry. Lear retires with a retinue of a hundred knights to live alternately with Goneril and Regan, who promptly turn on him.

The play has a second plot that runs in parallel. The Earl of Gloucester has two sons: Edgar, the legitimate heir, and Edmund, his illegitimate son. Edmund convinces Gloucester that Edgar is plotting against him. Edgar is forced into exile and survives by disguising himself as a mad beggar. Gloucester is later blinded for trying to help Lear. By the end of the play, eight major characters are dead.

Shakespeare wrote King Lear around 1606, basing it partly on a chronicle history that ended with Cordelia restoring Lear to his throne. Shakespeare changed the ending: Cordelia is hanged in prison, and Lear dies holding her body. For more than a century after the Restoration the play was performed only with a happier ending; Shakespeare's text was put back on the English stage in the nineteenth century and has been since.

angleCards.title: The love test.
angleCards.text: The whole play begins with one decision: Lear stages a public competition to see which daughter loves him most. Watch what that decision says about him, and what each daughter actually does with it.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read King Lear as a study of what Lear's love test asks for, what each daughter does in response, and what the play thinks of a man who needs love to be performed.

angleCards.title: Madness on the heath.
angleCards.text: The middle of the play takes Lear out into a storm on a heath, half mad, talking to a beggar who is really a duke's son in disguise. Those scenes are the centre of the play and the part everyone remembers.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow the storm scenes on the heath — Lear's collapse into madness, the Fool, the disguised Edgar — as the play's moral and philosophical centre.

angleCards.title: Fathers and children.
angleCards.text: Lear has three daughters. Gloucester has two sons. Both fathers are betrayed by the children they trusted and helped by the ones they cast off. The two plots mirror each other deliberately.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read the Lear and Gloucester plots together as parallel studies of fathers misreading their children, and decide what the play makes of the symmetry.

angleCards.title: The ending.
angleCards.text: Shakespeare changed his sources to make the ending bleaker than anything in English drama before it. The change matters: it is the line in the play scholars argue about most.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read King Lear with attention to its ending — Shakespeare's decision to kill Cordelia — and to what difference that single change makes to the meaning of the play.

cast.name: King Lear
cast.description: An old king, somewhere over eighty, who decides to retire and divide the kingdom among his daughters. He is used to being obeyed and cannot bear being contradicted. He has spent his life as the centre of the world and has no idea how to be anything else. The play is the storm that takes him apart and the unbearable scene at the end where he is briefly given back what he loved.

cast.name: Cordelia
cast.description: Lear's favourite child, who refuses to flatter him in the opening scene and is disinherited. She leaves with the King of France. She returns at the head of a French army to rescue her father from her sisters, and the play kills her almost casually in the last scene.

cast.name: Goneril and Regan
cast.description: Two married daughters who give the speeches their father wanted to hear and take the kingdom he offered them. Each is brutal in her own way: Goneril cold and managerial, Regan colder and more cruel. They both fall in love, in turn, with Edmund, and that competition is what finally destroys them.

cast.name: The Earl of Gloucester
cast.description: A vassal of Lear with two sons — the legitimate Edgar and the illegitimate Edmund. He believes Edmund's lies about Edgar, disinherits the wrong son, and is later blinded for trying to help the old king. His suffering is the second-string echo of Lear's.

cast.name: Edmund
cast.description: The illegitimate son, sharp, ambitious, and completely free of conventional morality. He frames his brother, betrays his father, and seduces both of Lear's older daughters at the same time. He is one of Shakespeare's most articulate villains and the closest thing the play has to an Iago.

cast.name: Edgar
cast.description: Forced into exile by Edmund's lies and surviving as a half-naked beggar named Poor Tom. He guides his blinded father across the heath and fights his brother in the last act. He is the play's only sustained voice of decency, and the one who is given the closing lines.

acclaim.quote: Of all Shakespeare's plays King Lear is the one in which he stands most decidedly on a level with Aeschylus and Sophocles.
King Lear is the greatest of Shakespeare's plays, in respect of imagination and pathos; the greatest, in absolute power.

whyItMatters.title: The Ending Shakespeare Chose
whyItMatters.body: Shakespeare did not invent the Lear story. He inherited it from Holinshed and from an older anonymous play called The True Chronicle History of King Leir, both of which end with Lear restored to his throne and Cordelia alive. Shakespeare changed it. He has Cordelia hanged in her prison cell, off stage, by Edmund's orders. He has Lear come on stage holding her body and asking why a horse and a dog have life and she has no breath at all. He has Lear die a moment later, looking at her lips for a movement that is not there. For more than a hundred years after the Restoration the English stage refused to perform this ending — Nahum Tate rewrote the play in 1681 with Cordelia married to Edgar — and the Tate version was the one Dr Johnson and most of Romantic England saw. The Shakespeare ending came back in the nineteenth century and has been the standard since. The disagreement is what the play does to its sources: it refuses the consolation the source material offers and asks whether the audience can tolerate the world without it. Lear is the play where Shakespeare bet his audience could.

whyItMatters.title: The Storm on the Heath
whyItMatters.body: The middle of King Lear is a stretch of three or four scenes in which Lear, half mad, runs out into a storm with his Fool and meets the disguised Edgar pretending to be a lunatic beggar. The four of them — old king, fool, beggar, and the loyal Kent in his own disguise — stand on a heath in the rain at night and talk about justice, nakedness, madness, animals, and what a human being is when you take everything else away. Lear strips off his clothes. He puts an imaginary court on trial. He decides that 'unaccommodated man is no more but such a poor, bare, forked animal' as the half-naked Tom on the heath. These scenes are routinely called the centre of King Lear and frequently called the centre of all of Shakespeare. They are also where the play earns its reputation for cosmic bleakness: the king and the gods and the order of the kingdom are all stripped down in the same storm.

whyItMatters.title: Two Plots, One Question
whyItMatters.body: King Lear has the most elaborate subplot of any Shakespeare tragedy. The Gloucester story — old father, two sons, one legitimate and trusting, one illegitimate and plotting, the father blinded for siding with the wrong children — runs in parallel to the Lear story for the entire play and crosses into it in the middle. The two plots ask the same question from slightly different angles: what does a parent owe a child, what does a child owe a parent, and what happens when both sides fail. Lear gets his test wrong by demanding flattery; Gloucester gets his wrong by trusting the wrong son. Each father is helped, when it matters most, by the child he disinherited. Each father has to lose almost everything before he can see. The decision to run the two stories side by side — unique among Shakespeare's tragedies — is what gives King Lear its weight: the play is not about a single mistake but about a pattern, and the pattern can happen to anyone.
